concept_summary: The 1913 initial-rate law for invertase action states that the reaction velocity is proportional to the enzyme amount and rises with substrate concentration toward a plateau. In modern notation v = Vmax*S/(Km+S): S and Km share one concentration unit, Vmax is the plateau rate reached as S grows, and Km is the substrate concentration giving exactly half of Vmax.

controls.label: Vmax (plateau rate)
controls.meaning: Rate approached as substrate concentration becomes large; sets the height of the plateau.

controls.label: Km (half-saturation constant)
controls.meaning: Substrate concentration at which v equals half of Vmax; same concentration unit as S.

controls.label: Substrate concentration S
controls.meaning: Concentration of substrate offered to the enzyme; drives the saturation curve.

equations.explanation: Transcribed 1913 initial-rate expression: velocity is proportional to enzyme amount Phi and to [S]/([S]+k). The modern teaching form v = Vmax*S/(Km+S) is the same shape with Vmax = C*Phi and Km = k.
Dividing the rate law by Vmax isolates the dimensionless saturation fraction, which equals 1/2 when S = Km.

explanation_steps.body: The 1913 paper writes the initial velocity as proportional to the enzyme amount Phi and to [S]/([S]+k). The modern teaching form v = Vmax*S/(Km+S) keeps that shape: Vmax = C*Phi collects the proportionality constant and enzyme amount, and Km = k is the substrate concentration at half saturation. Because S and Km are added, they must carry the same concentration unit.
explanation_steps.heading: The initial-rate law

explanation_steps.body: At small S the denominator is dominated by Km, so v is roughly (Vmax/Km)*S: the rate grows almost linearly with substrate. As S grows past Km the denominator is dominated by S, the fraction S/(Km+S) approaches 1, and v flattens toward the plateau Vmax. The gap Vmax - v shrinks but never reaches zero at finite S.
explanation_steps.heading: Why the curve saturates

explanation_steps.body: Setting S = Km makes the fraction Km/(Km+Km) = 1/2, so v = Vmax/2. This is the operational meaning of Km: it is read off the curve as the substrate concentration giving half the plateau rate, and it is a concentration, not a rate.
explanation_steps.heading: Reading Km off the curve

explorations.change: Set Km = 1 and Vmax = 1, then move S from 0 up to 20 in steps of about 1.
explorations.observe: v starts near 0, passes 0.5 at S = 1, and by S = 8 is about 0.89 while the gap Vmax - v has fallen to about 0.11.
explorations.why: The fraction S/(Km+S) rises steeply while S < Km and then bends over, so the rate approaches the plateau without ever exceeding it.

explorations.change: Keep S = 4 fixed and raise Km from 0.1 to 10.
explorations.observe: v falls from about 0.976 toward about 0.286 as Km grows, and the saturation fraction S/(Km+S) falls with it.
explorations.why: Km sits in the denominator, so a larger Km means more substrate is needed to reach the same fraction of the plateau; at fixed S the enzyme looks less saturated.

grounding.paper_title: The Kinetics of Invertase Action (1913), Johnson and Goody translation

source_claims.claim: The initial rate is proportional to the enzyme amount and to [S]/([S]+k), with C a proportionality constant.

teaching_simplifications: The modern symbols Vmax and Km are teaching notation for C*Phi and k; the excerpt supplies only the transcribed equation and the note that C is a proportionality constant.
The fixed substrate scan [0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8] and the gap Vmax - v are pedagogical constructions, not data from the 1913 paper.
The numeric ranges of the sliders (Vmax, Km, S) are chosen for display and are not experimental values reported in the excerpt.

limitations: This is a toy evaluation of the rate law, not a reproduction of the 1913 invertase experiments; no measured velocities or concentrations from the paper are used.
The excerpt supplies only the transcribed equation and the statement that C is a proportionality constant, so the identification Vmax = C*Phi and Km = k is a teaching interpretation.
Km is not generally a binding dissociation constant; it is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal rate under the stated initial-rate assumptions and can reflect multiple kinetic steps.
The model assumes a single substrate, initial-rate conditions, and no product inhibition, reversibility, or enzyme inactivation; those effects are outside the excerpt.
The line view sweeps S only up to the slider maximum of 20, so the plateau is approached but never exactly attained.

title: Initial-Rate Kinetics: v = Vmax*S/(Km+S)
why_it_matters: This rate law is the standard starting point for describing enzyme kinetics: it explains why reaction velocity rises with substrate but levels off, and it defines Km as a concentration that reports how much substrate is needed for half-maximal activity. Getting the units and the half-saturation reading right is essential before fitting real velocity data or comparing enzymes.
